summary.text: Taking \(n=7\), the prescribed restriction on \(x\) forces \(x\ge 3\); since \(x\le y\le z\), all three summands are at least \(3\), so their sum is at least \(9\), contradicting \(x+y+z=7\).

full_proof.text:
Let the conjecture be understood as the conjunction of the following two assertions:

1. For every integer \(n>5\), there is at least one ordered triple \(0<x\le y\le z\) with \(x+y+z=n\) for which
\[
2x-1,\quad 2y-1,\quad 2z-1,\quad 2xy-1,\quad 2xz-1,\quad 2yz-1
\]
are all prime.

2. Moreover, for every integer \(n>6\), such a representation can be chosen with
\[
x\in\{3,4,6,10,15\}.
\]

We disprove the conjunction by showing that its second assertion fails already at \(n=7\).

Suppose, for contradiction, that the conjecture were true. Since \(7>6\), its “moreover” clause would provide positive integers \(x,y,z\) such that
\[
x+y+z=7,\qquad x\le y\le z,
\]
with
\[
x\in\{3,4,6,10,15\},
\]
and with all six of the required numbers prime.

Every element of the displayed five-element set is at least \(3\). Indeed, this is immediate by considering its five possible values: \(3,4,6,10,15\). Hence \(x\ge3\). From the required ordering \(x\le y\), it follows that \(y\ge3\). From \(y\le z\), it likewise follows that \(z\ge3\). Therefore
\[
x+y+z\ge 3+3+3=9.
\]
But the same triple was required to satisfy \(x+y+z=7\), which is impossible because \(9>7\).

Thus no ordered positive triple summing to \(7\) can have its first coordinate in \(\{3,4,6,10,15\}\), independently of any primality conditions. Consequently the “moreover” assertion is false at \(n=7\). Since the stated conjecture is the conjunction of that assertion with the positivity assertion for \(a(n)\), the failure of this one conjunct disproves the whole conjecture.
